answer:
The assigned source cannot determine a propagation speed c. It supplies x(n)=nL for integer n>=0 and says that L is a length scale. It supplies neither a time map t(n) nor a clock interval. These are the only assigned source facts used here. The assumptions below are proposals, and their consequences are conditional algebra rather than assigned physics.

The source fixes the position difference x(n+1)-x(n)=L. The index n counts positions; it has no assigned time unit. A difference in position per index step has units of length, whereas speed requires length divided by time. Converting the count into elapsed time is therefore an additional choice. This establishes a missing assumption in the derivation, not an inconsistency in the position formula.

One proposed clock is t(n)=n tau, with tau>0 a finite time interval measured, for example, in seconds. This clock is not in the assigned source. Under this proposal, the signed displacement per elapsed step is v_n=[x(n+1)-x(n)]/[t(n+1)-t(n)]=L/tau for every n>=0. For any integers 0<=m<n, the same interval ratio is [x(n)-x(m)]/[t(n)-t(m)]=L/tau. Its units are length/time; metres for L and seconds for tau would give metres/second. If a positive length scale L>0 is additionally assumed, this ratio is a positive step speed v=L/tau. More generally the magnitude of the signed step velocity is |L|/tau. These are interval ratios at sampled events. An instantaneous derivative or motion between the events requires a further trajectory or interpolation assumption. The expression x(n)/t(n) must not be evaluated at n=0; the consecutive-step ratio above has no such problem.

The speed is not identifiable from the position sequence. Under the proposed positive-scale case L>0, every proposed positive value V can be obtained by choosing tau=L/V. In particular, tau and 2 tau leave all assigned x(n) unchanged while giving step speeds L/tau and L/(2 tau). Thus the source does not select a unique numerical speed, a clock scale, or c. A second admissible proposed clock, t(n)=n^2 tau with tau>0, is strictly increasing for the assigned nonnegative integers and gives v_n=L/[(2n+1)tau]. The same positions then have variable step velocities. The positive-index average ratio from the origin is L/(n tau) for n>0, which is a different quantity from the consecutive-step ratio. These alternative clocks are counterexamples to uniqueness, not evidence that either clock describes a real process.

For a fixed proposed L>0 and the uniform clock, tau approaching zero through positive values makes L/tau grow without bound, and tau approaching infinity makes it approach zero. Tau=0 itself yields no defined step speed. These are algebraic limits within the proposed model; they imply no physical permission for arbitrarily large propagation speed and no physical upper bound. With the quadratic proposed clock and fixed tau>0, the consecutive-step ratio approaches zero as n grows. If L=0, the sampled displacement ratios are zero for a positive time interval, but sampled positions alone still do not determine motion between events.

To identify the conditional ratio with c, state what c denotes and add a justified link to these indexed events. If c is merely a model name for the step ratio, an explicit definition c:=L/tau permits that notation without determining a numerical value or a physical law. If c denotes an independently defined physical propagation constant, the missing evidence includes a calibrated time relation for the indexed events, the applicable length scale and units, a definition of what propagates and which interval is measured, and independent justification or measurement that its interval speed equals that constant in the stated regime. Stipulating tau=L/c imports c into the clock choice; substituting it into L/tau then reproduces the stipulation and does not independently derive c. The assigned packet provides none of that timed physical evidence. No validated physics or Aether-Flow result follows from this answer.
